articles.summary: The Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on being confused with James Nesbitt, his own Sliding Doors moment and a new perspective since turning 60. How often do you get asked to recite that WH Auden poem from Four Weddings and a Funeral, and can you do it from memory right now?
body: In Steve Coogan ’s Paul Calf’s Video Diary, your character praises Orson Welles’ The Trial for its “tremendous energy”, while Paul says he would “rather watch Dave Lee Travis playing Macbeth”. What’s your actual opinion of The Trial [by Franz Kafka]? AdrianH1 God, it’s a long time since I’ve read that. I read a lot of those books in my younger days, but probably, like a lot of people, even those who are graduates of English literature, I’d be hard pushed these days to tell you what it was about, other than the persecution of some minor character.

As a popular jobbing actor, you have a massive list of credits. Has anyone ever come up to you to express their appreciation for a certain role and you had no idea what they were on about? Kevcoe No. It’s always heartwarming when somebody comes up and offers their congratulations on something a little bit lower down the pecking order. Fortunately, people rarely ever come up to tell me that they thought I was shit in something. I quite often get Paul Calf’s Video Diary, and that Macbeth line. To be frank, I can’t quite remember the context.

articles.title: Charlie Brooker’s New Netflix Series Gets Title, ‘Blackmere,’ as Rory Kinnear Joins Cast and First-Look Photos Revealed
articles.summary: Charlie Brooker’s new Netflix series has revealed its title — “Blackmere” — not to be confused with the writer and producer’s other show for the streamer, “Black Mirror.” Netflix announced the show’s title, some first-look images and the news that Rory Kinnear (“The Diplomat,” “Black Mirror”) has…
body: Charlie Brooker ‘s new Netflix series has revealed its title — “Blackmere” — not to be confused with the writer and producer’s other show for the streamer, “ Black Mirror.”

“Blackmere” was created and written by Brooker, with co-writers including Ben Caudell, Jason Hazeley, Emer Kenny, Daniel Maier and Joel Morris, plus additional material by Victoria Asare Archer. Brooker executive produces alongside Jessica Rhoades and Annabel Jones, with Mark Kinsella co-executive producing and Richard Webb producing. Al Campbell is the series director.

Brooker’s new series was first announced last year as the “Untitled Charlie Brooker Project.” “I’m beyond thrilled to be saying these words for the press release. I’ve dreamt of providing a quote ever since I was a young foetus, and now here I am doing it,” Brooker said at the time. “I’d pinch myself, but like all of us, I’m terrified that if I do that, I might wake up and discover 2025 has all been a magical dream. Please watch my show. I am begging you.”
Besides “Blackmere,” Brooker’s highly successful “Black Mirror” is set to return to Netflix for an eighth season, which started production this summer.

articles.title: Global release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZA
articles.summary: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website. NAZA, the award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is set to be released in cinemas in more than 50…
body: The film, which the Guardian produced, premiered at the Venice film festival earlier this month, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

After screenings in Bologna and at the San Sebastián film festival, the film will receive its North American premiere on Saturday at the New York film festival before opening four days later at the IFC Center in New York City. On 9 October it will expand to Los Angeles and other key US cities before a national rollout.

A theatrical release in partnership with MK2 Films is also planned in 55 other territories, including the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Canada, Hong Kong, Brazil, Turkey, Thailand, France, Spain, Germany, Turkey, Central America and the Middle East.
After its run in cinemas, the film will stream on the Guardian’s website, for free, as part of the news organisation’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism.

articles.title: Post your questions for Zach Braff
articles.summary: Known to many as JD in Scrubs, Zach Braff has forged a path as a successful writer and director since the release of his acclaimed 2004 indie film Garden State. Now’s your chance to ask him your burning questions.
body: There’s much more to Zach Braff than hospital scrubs and hair that could keep the entire mousse industry afloat. His second career as a film-maker got off to quite the start with his 2004 directorial debut Garden State, which he also wrote and starred in. Shot for just $2.5m, it went on to make more than $35m worldwide, pick up over three dozen award nominations and earn Braff a Grammy for compiling its soundtrack, featuring the Shins, Coldplay and Nick Drake.

Then as a film actor he has also popped up in everything from 2000 gay ensemble comedy-drama The Broken Hearts Club, alongside Timothy Olyphant, and 2006 romantic drama The Last Kiss, opposite Jacinda Barrett, to 2006 workplace romcom The Ex, with Jason Bateman, and 2016 John Steinbeck adaptation In Dubious Battle, directed by James Franco.

articles.title: Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek Says Bob Iger Ran ‘Relentless Three-Year Campaign’ to Fire Him: ‘Made It Seem as If I Had Committed Some Terrible Offense’
articles.summary: Former Disney CEO Bob Chapek claims his predecessor-turned-successor Bob Iger underwent a “relentless three-year campaign to push me out” after initially appointing him to the job.
body: “From the moment he announced my appointment, he clearly regretted it and seemed to initiate a relentless three-year campaign to push me out,” Chapek writes of Iger. “From day one as CEO, I had respected the board’s decision to have him remain as executive chairman, directing creative endeavors and overseeing the transition until late 2021. I’d always made it clear I had big shoes to fill. But I’d never expected to endure a drawn-out, purposeful undoing of my leadership.”
Disney declined to comment Thursday. Iger declined to comment via a representative at Thrive Capital, where Iger is now a partner.
Disney insiders are said to view Chapek’s book as a “revisionist” account of the events that transpired.

Published by Simon & Schuster, “Behind the Castle Walls” is set to release Sept. 29. While Chapek is making the rounds promoting the book with today’s Vanity Fair excerpt and an interview published by the Wall Street Journal Wednesday, according to industry sources, the title remains in stiff competition with Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan’s upcoming unauthorized “The House of Mouse: Bob Iger and The War of Succession at Disney,” which is slated for release on Dec. 1, 2026.

articles.title: ‘I’m a writer but then nobody’s perfect’: how Billy Wilder conquered Hollywood
articles.summary: From émigré roots to a titan of modern cinema, penning classics such as Double Indemnity, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, a new retrospective celebrates the father of film noir’s incredible career. Like all survivors, Billy Wilder never forgot where he came from or what he had left behind.
body: Wilder was an inveterate self-mythologiser, a film-maker with a brand long before there were opportunities for promotion through Instagram accounts and chicken shop dates. He told a story of living in Berlin during his fledgling years in show business and being kept awake all night by “a toilet that was on the blink”.
“I would lie there and listen to it, and since I was young and romantic, I’d imagine it was a beautiful waterfall – just to get my mind off the monotony of it and the thought of it being a can.”

Most of us would have called a plumber but the aspiring young film-maker chose instead to use the incident as fuel for perhaps the greatest body of work in cinema’s golden age. This is the man who made Double Indemnity, the archetypal film noir and the genre’s zenith, a film often imitated but never equalled. He was responsible for Some Like It Hot, a movie routinely voted the greatest comedy ever made, while his Sunset Boulevard is generally acknowledged as the best film about show business. The Apartment, arguably his magnum opus, is rightly considered one of the greatest films in the history of the medium.

Wilder was an inveterate self-mythologiser, a film-maker with a brand long before there were opportunities for promotion through Instagram accounts and chicken shop dates.

articles.title: Fantastic Fest 2026: Pathetic Fallacy, Upiro, Kick On, What Happened to Doris?
articles.summary: Our final four films from Fantastic Fest include a trippy vision with Kid Cudi, a Spanish vampire flick, and an Aussie Green Room.
body: Our final dispatch from this year’s Fantastic Fest is indicative of the remarkable range of the programming at the world’s best genre event: There’s a Spanish vampire movie, an Australian thriller, an American ghost story, and something almost indescribably built on dream logic. Three of them are worth a look when they get international release.

Cudi plays Asher, who has a meet-cute, romance, and tragedy in the first ten minutes of the film. The object of his affection is Iris ( Jessica Rothe, in her third Fantastic Fest flick just this year), and her passing destroys Asher. Mortimer holds a scene in which she dies in Asher’s embrace a remarkably long time, her breathing getting shallower over about a full two minutes, one of the first signs that this is a filmmaker who isn’t scared to do things a little differently.

articles.title: Bob Iger Reveals That He Wrote a Six-Page Letter to Josh D’Amaro and Left It In His Desk
articles.summary: In an interview with Harvard Business Review, the former Disney chief also said that the challenges facing CEOs are tougher than ever: "We live in a state of almost perpetual crisis."
body: When Bob Iger officially stepped aside as CEO of The Walt Disney Co. earlier this year to hand the keys to the kingdom to Josh D’Amaro, he decided to take a cue from an Oval Office tradition.

“I decided I would write my successor a letter and leave it in his desk, as we’ve heard Presidents of the United States have done recently. And I wanted it to be short. It ended up being six pages long,” Iger said in an interview published by the Harvard Business Review on Thursday. “One of the things that I did write is be aware of how much influence you have over the company. You’re inheriting a company that’s 103 years old, and you think, well, maybe there’s nothing that any one leader can do to change it or influence it.”

“But be aware of the fact that you have enormous influence over it, and you can exert that influence quickly and sometimes almost inadvertently just by having the title,” he added. “That there’s a tremendous amount of responsibility. And I think if you are aware of the influence you have, then you act more responsibly, because you are aware of just how powerful that influence can be. It’s just so important.”

articles.title: Taylor Tomlinson on the Messy Demise of Her Late Night Career (Exclusive Excerpt)
articles.summary: In her new collection of essays, 'Actually, Nevermind,' the top comic and former host of CBS' 'After Midnight' writes candidly about a deeply personal decision that left her "shaking with shame."
body: My health improved during season two, but my immune system was still fragile in a way it had never been before, still reeling from the supermassive hit it had taken. I was a full-blown germaphobe now and still came down with anything that was going around. Every time I got sick, I panicked; I was going to let everyone down. People only liked me for what I could do. If I couldn’t work, I was worthless. If I didn’t perform, I was alone.

I had no one to blame but myself. I was the insatiable pit seeking validation, taking a full-time TV job on weekdays and chasing myself onto cross-country flights every weekend. I was the one not taking care of me, not valuing myself enough to rest.

I realized this wasn’t just a bad year, a tough moment, a difficult chapter. It was the inevitable result of a decade of over-working myself. My ambition and my body had been at war for years, and it was finally coming to a head. My body slammed on the brakes, and I flew over the handlebars. Only when I found myself in a crumpled heap, head bleeding, limbs twisted and turned, did I accept it. I needed a break.
